title: 26  Model Evaluation and Selection Review Questions
text:
Warning: AI-assisted materials These materials were developed with assistance from AI tools. All content has been reviewed and edited by the instructor, who takes final responsibility for its accuracy, clarity, and appropriateness for the course. Students should treat these materials as instructor-reviewed course content while applying the same critical judgment they would use with any technical material. Please report any suspected errors or unclear explanations to ghunt@wm.edu.

These questions accompany 005_evaluation_and_model_selection_v3.ipynb. Answers are hidden in collapsible sections.

26.0.1 Question 1
An evaluation dataset \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{eval}}\) did not influence a fitted model \(\hat f\), but it was collected from a population different from the one where the model will be deployed. Does \(M(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{eval}},\hat f)\) estimate the desired deployment performance?


Answer

Not necessarily. Independence from the fitted model prevents reuse of evaluation information, but the evaluation observations must also represent the target population. Otherwise the metric estimates performance on the evaluation population rather than on the deployment population. Thus we need both separation from model building and a distribution appropriate to the intended use.



26.0.2 Question 2
A student argues: “The fitting algorithm minimized training error, so training error is the most direct measure of how good the fitted model is.” Diagnose the mistake.


Answer

Minimizing training error makes it a direct measure of fit to the observed sample, but that is why it is not neutral evidence about new data. The algorithm searched for a function that performs well on those observations, rewarding improvements caused by reproducible signal and improvements caused by sample-specific variation. Generalization asks which improvements persist on new observations, so it requires data that did not determine the fit.



26.0.3 Question 3
Let \(\hat f_d\) be the least-squares fit among polynomials of degree at most \(d\), using a fixed training dataset. Prove that \[
\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}}(\hat f_{d+1})
\le
\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}}(\hat f_d).
\] Does the same inequality necessarily hold for evaluation MSE?


Answer

Every polynomial of degree at most \(d\) is also a polynomial of degree at most \(d+1\): set the coefficient of \(x^{d+1}\) to zero. Thus the degree-\((d+1)\) optimization searches over a set containing every degree-\(d\) candidate. Its minimum training MSE cannot be larger.
No analogous conclusion follows for evaluation MSE. The additional coefficient is selected using the training sample and may fit sample-specific noise that does not recur in the evaluation data.



26.0.4 Question 4
In the lecture’s cartoon of training and evaluation error versus model complexity, describe the typical behavior in three regions: low, intermediate, and high complexity. Identify underfitting and overfitting, and explain why the evaluation curve’s U shape is a pattern rather than a theorem.


Answer

At low complexity, the class cannot represent enough of the signal, so both errors are high: this is underfitting. At intermediate complexity, the model captures more signal and evaluation error is often near its minimum. At high complexity, training error can continue downward while evaluation error rises because the model increasingly fits sample-specific variation: this is overfitting.
The U shape is not guaranteed because observed errors contain sampling noise and different data-generating processes, model classes, and fitting procedures can produce different curves.



26.0.5 Question 5
An analyst randomly splits observations into \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{train}}\) and \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{eval}}\), but computes means and standard deviations using all observations before the split. The model uses those values to standardize its inputs. Is the subsequent evaluation reasonable?


Answer

No. The fitted model depends on summary information from \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{eval}}\), so the evaluation observations have influenced model building. Fit the standardization parameters using only \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{train}}\), then apply that fixed transformation to \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{eval}}\). In cross-validation, repeat this fitting step inside every training fold; a pipeline can enforce that order.



26.0.6 Question 6
Five-fold cross-validation is used. How many times is each observation used for evaluation and for training?


Answer

Each observation belongs to one evaluation fold, so it is used for evaluation once. It belongs to the training portion for each of the other four fits, so it is used for training four times.



26.0.7 Question 7
A false argument says: “Fold \(\mathcal F_j\) is omitted when fitting \(\hat f^{(-j)}\), so the \(k\) cross-validation scores \(e_1,\ldots,e_k\) are independent.” Identify the false step.


Answer

Omitting \(\mathcal F_j\) from its corresponding fit supports evaluating \(\hat f^{(-j)}\) on that fold. It does not make scores from different folds independent. The training sets \(\mathcal D\setminus\mathcal F_j\) overlap heavily, and every score is a function of the same original dataset. Consequently the fold scores are generally dependent, and their sample standard deviation is not automatically a standard error for their mean.



26.0.8 Question 8
After \(k\)-fold CV, a collaborator asks which fitted function \[
\hat f^{(-1)},\ldots,\hat f^{(-k)}
\] should be deployed. What is the correct response?


Answer

None of the fold-specific functions is ordinarily deployed. They are temporary fits used to estimate the performance of the fixed fitting procedure \(A\). Once the procedure is settled, fit \[
\hat f_{\mathrm{final}}=A(\mathcal D)
\] on all available training data and deploy that result. CV supplied evidence about the procedure, not an independent evaluation of this particular final fit.



26.0.9 Question 9
A dataset contains \(N=200\) observations and is evaluated using five-fold CV. At what training-sample size is the procedure directly evaluated in each fold?


Answer

Each fit uses four of the five folds, hence \[
200\left(\frac45\right)=160
\] training observations. CV evaluates several outputs of the procedure trained on 160 observations. The final model uses all 200 observations and is a different fitted function, so the CV score is not its direct test error. It is an estimate of procedure-level performance at the fold training size and is often informative about the final full-data fit.



26.0.10 Question 10
Three polynomial procedures have validation MSEs



Degree \(d\)
1
3
5




\(e_d\)
4.8
2.1
2.7



Compute the selected degree \(\hat d\).


Answer

The minimum validation MSE is \(2.1\), so \[
\hat d=\arg\min_{d\in\{1,3,5\}}e_d=3.
\]



26.0.11 Question 11
For every fixed \(\lambda\), the candidate \[
\hat f_\lambda=A_\lambda(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{train}})
\] is evaluated on separate validation data. Explain why \(e_\lambda=M(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{val}},\hat f_\lambda)\) can reasonably estimate that candidate’s performance while the winning score \(e_{\hat\lambda}\) is usually optimistic after selection.


Answer

For a fixed \(\lambda\), validation observations did not determine \(\hat f_\lambda\), so their metric provides fresh-data evidence for that candidate. Selection changes the situation: \(\hat\lambda\) is chosen because \(e_{\hat\lambda}\) is the most favorable among several noisy estimates. The winning value can be low because of genuinely better performance and because its validation noise happened to be favorable. It has therefore lost its role as an independent evaluation of the selected result.



26.0.12 Question 12
Two candidates have the same true error, \(1\). Their validation errors are \[
e_1=1+\varepsilon_1,
\qquad
e_2=1+\varepsilon_2,
\] where \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) are independent and each equals \(-0.2\) or \(0.2\) with probability \(1/2\). Compute \(\mathbb E[\min(e_1,e_2)]\) and interpret the result.


Answer

The four pairs of noise values are equally likely. The minimum validation error is \(0.8\) in three cases and \(1.2\) only when both noise values equal \(0.2\). Hence \[
\mathbb E[\min(e_1,e_2)]
=\frac34(0.8)+\frac14(1.2)=0.9.
\] Each candidate’s validation error is centered at its true error, but selecting the smaller estimate produces an expected reported value below the common true error. This is selection optimism.



26.0.13 Question 13
Why can searching a larger candidate set \(\Lambda\), or repeatedly changing \(\Lambda\) after inspecting validation results, increase validation-set overfitting? Give an answer in terms of noisy performance estimates and the larger procedure’s capacity.


Answer

Each candidate has a noisy validation estimate. A larger search creates more opportunities to encounter an unusually favorable estimate and select it. Revising the search after inspecting results adapts the candidate set itself to the validation data. Both actions increase the capacity of the meta-procedure to exploit validation noise, so the winning score can become more optimistic even if the selected model’s true performance does not improve.



26.0.14 Question 14
In a three-way split, state the role of each dataset: \[
\mathcal D_{\mathrm{train}},\qquad
\mathcal D_{\mathrm{val}},\qquad
\mathcal D_{\mathrm{test}}.
\] For each one, say whether it may influence candidate parameters, the selected \(\hat\lambda\), and the final reported performance estimate.


Answer

\(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{train}}\) fits candidate parameters. \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{val}}\) compares candidates and therefore influences \(\hat\lambda\). Both are model-building data. After selection, they may be combined to refit the selected procedure.
\(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{test}}\) should influence neither candidate parameters nor \(\hat\lambda\). It is used only after model building is complete to produce the final reported performance estimate.



26.0.15 Question 15
After selecting \(\hat\lambda\) using validation data, why is it reasonable to refit \(A_{\hat\lambda}\) on \[
\mathcal D_{\mathrm{train}}\cup\mathcal D_{\mathrm{val}}
\] before evaluating on \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{test}}\)? Why does this not invalidate the test evaluation?


Answer

Validation data have already participated in model building by selecting \(\hat\lambda\). Once that choice is fixed, combining them with the original training data gives the final coefficient fit more observations. This does not invalidate test evaluation because \(\mathcal D_{\mathrm{test}}\) remains absent from fitting, validation, selection, and refitting.



26.0.16 Question 16
Before splitting its data, an analyst selects the 20 features having the largest correlations with the response. The analyst then performs a train/validation/test split and reports test error. Identify the leakage and give the correct workflow.


Answer

Feature selection used every response, including test responses, so the selected feature set—and hence the final model—depends on test data. The later split cannot remove that dependence.
First reserve the test set. Select features using only model-building data. If validation or CV is used, repeat response-based feature selection inside each training split or fold. Apply the resulting selected-feature rule to the corresponding validation data, and leave test data untouched until the final evaluation.

27.0.1 Question 1
The lecture begins with the risk \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_{(X,Y)\sim P}[\ell(Y,s(X))].
\] What is the target \(s^*\) trying to find?


Answer

The target is \[
s^*=\arg\min_s R(s),
\] the score function with smallest expected loss under the true data-generating distribution \(P\).



27.0.2 Question 2
Starting from \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_{(X,Y)}[\ell(Y,s(X))],
\] use the law of total expectation to derive the conditional-risk form \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_X[L_X(s(X))],
\qquad
L_x(t)=\mathbb E[\ell(Y,t)\mid X=x].
\]


Answer

By the law of total expectation, \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_X\left[\mathbb E[\ell(Y,s(X))\mid X]\right].
\] After conditioning on \(X=x\), the value \(s(X)\) becomes \(s(x)\), so the inner expectation is \[
\mathbb E[\ell(Y,s(x))\mid X=x].
\] Defining \[
L_x(t)=\mathbb E[\ell(Y,t)\mid X=x]
\] gives \[
R(s)=\mathbb E_X[L_X(s(X))].
\]



27.0.3 Question 3
The lecture says unrestricted risk minimization can be done pointwise. Why are we free to choose each value of \(s(x)\) separately for each value of \(x\)?


Answer

The key assumption is that the function class is unrestricted so that the values \(s(x)\) can be chosen independently at different inputs. If we have no restrictions on \(s\) then we can do this. After all, what is a function other than an assignment of \(s(x)\) to each \(x\)? If we can choose any function then we can choose each \(s(x)\) completely separately for each \(x\).



27.0.4 Question 4
We showed that \[
s^*(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{t}\mathbb{E}[\ell(Y,t)\mid X=x].
\] For squared-loss regression, this is \[
s^*(x)=\arg\min_t\mathbb E[(Y-t)^2\mid X=x].
\] Show that this is equivalent to: \[
s^*(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x].
\]


Answer

Expand the conditional objective: \[
\mathbb E[(Y-t)^2\mid X=x]
=\mathbb E[Y^2\mid X=x]-2t\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]+t^2.
\] Differentiate with respect to \(t\): \[
-2\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]+2t.
\] Setting this equal to zero gives \[
t=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\] The second derivative is \(2>0\), so this critical point is the unique minimizer.



27.0.5 Question 5
At a particular input value \(x\), suppose the conditional distribution of \(Y\mid X=x\) assigns probability \(0.25\) to \(0\) and probability \(0.75\) to \(4\). Under squared loss, compute the optimal prediction \(s^*(x)\).


Answer

Under squared loss, \[
s^*(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\] Here \[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=0(0.25)+4(0.75)=3.
\] So the optimal prediction is \(s^*(x)=3\).



27.0.6 Question 6
Why is the exact-match estimator \[
\hat s(x)=\frac{1}{|\{n:x_n=x\}|}\sum_{n:x_n=x}y_n
\] usually not useful when \(X\in\mathbb R^D\) has a continuous distribution? Make a probabilistic argument based on the fact that: \[
\mathbb P(X=x)=0.
\]


Answer

If \(X\) has a continuous distribution, then for a fixed query point \(x\), \[
\mathbb P(X=x)=0.
\] With finitely many training observations, the probability of observing many, or even any, exact matches \(x_n=x\) is usually zero (or negligible). So exact conditional averaging is not usable. Moreover, this would only define predictions at points where we exactly have training data, but we want to be able to predict everywhere.



27.0.7 Question 7
Training inputs on the real line are \[
x_1=0,\quad x_2=1,\quad x_3=3,\quad x_4=4
\] with responses \[
y_1=2,\quad y_2=4,\quad y_3=10,\quad y_4=12.
\] Using Euclidean distance and query point \(x=2.6\), compute the nearest-neighbor regression prediction for \(m=2\).


Answer

The distances from \(x=2.6\) are \[
|0-2.6|=2.6,\quad |1-2.6|=1.6,\quad |3-2.6|=0.4,\quad |4-2.6|=1.4.
\] The two nearest inputs are \(3\) and \(4\), with responses \(10\) and \(12\). Therefore \[
\hat s_2(2.6)=\frac{10+12}{2}=11.
\]



27.0.8 Question 8
For the same data as Question 7, compute the nearest-neighbor regression prediction at \(x=2.6\) for \(m=4\). Compare it with the \(m=2\) prediction and state what changed.


Answer

For \(m=4\), all four responses are averaged: \[
\hat s_4(2.6)=\frac{2+4+10+12}{4}=7.
\] The \(m=2\) prediction was \(11\). Increasing \(m\) added farther-away points with smaller responses, so the prediction moved away from the local average near \(x=2.6\) and toward a more global average.



27.0.9 Question 9
In nearest-neighbor regression, how does the choice of \(m\) affect the flexibility of the fitted curve?


Answer

Smaller values of \(m\) make the fitted curve more flexible. Each prediction is based on only a few nearby points, so the curve can respond strongly to local changes in the training data.
Larger values of \(m\) make the fitted curve less flexible. Each prediction averages over more points, which smooths out local variation and produces a more stable curve.
So, decreasing \(m\) increases flexibility, while increasing \(m\) decreases flexibility.



27.0.10 Question 10
Compare nearest-neighbor regression and linear regression as estimators. Under squared loss, both methods target the conditional mean function \[
\mu(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\] State the main difference in how the two methods estimate it.


Answer

Linear regression estimates this target using a global parametric form, usually \(\mu(x)\approx w^\top x\). This imposes a single linear relationship across the feature space.
Nearest-neighbor regression estimates the target locally by averaging responses near the query point: \[
\hat s_m(x)=\frac1m\sum_{n\in\mathcal N_m(x)}y_n.
\] It does not impose a global linear form, but its behavior depends strongly on local neighborhoods and the choice of distance.



27.0.11 Question 11
In nearest-neighbor classification with classes \(\{1,\ldots,K\}\), show that minimizing 0-1 loss pointwise is equivalent to choosing the class with largest conditional probability \(\mathbb P(Y=c\mid X=x)\).


Answer

In classification, the prediction is a class label. Suppose that at a fixed input value \(x\), we predict class \(c\).
Under 0-1 loss, the loss is
\[
\ell(Y,c)=\mathbf{1}\{Y\neq c\}.
\]
This loss is \(0\) if the prediction is correct and \(1\) if the prediction is incorrect.
The conditional risk at \(x\) is the expected loss given \(X=x\):
\[
L_x(c)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\{Y\neq c\}\mid X=x].
\]
Because the expectation of an indicator is the probability of the event, this becomes
\[
L_x(c)=\mathbb P(Y\neq c\mid X=x).
\]
So, for a fixed \(x\), minimizing the conditional 0-1 risk means choosing the class \(c\) that makes the probability of misclassification as small as possible.
Now use the fact that, if we predict class \(c\), the only way to be correct is for \(Y=c\). Therefore,
\[
\mathbb P(Y\neq c\mid X=x)=1-\mathbb P(Y=c\mid X=x).
\]
Thus,
\[
L_x(c)=1-\mathbb P(Y=c\mid X=x).
\]
Since the \(1\) is the same for every possible class \(c\), minimizing \(L_x(c)\) is the same as maximizing \(\mathbb P(Y=c\mid X=x)\).
Therefore, the pointwise optimal classifier is
\[
f^*(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le c\le K} \mathbb P(Y=c\mid X=x).
\]
This is the Bayes classifier. It says that, at each input \(x\), the optimal prediction under 0-1 loss is the most likely class conditional on \(X=x\).



27.0.12 Question 12
For nearest-neighbor classification, prove that the score \[
\hat s_{m,c}(x)=\frac1m\sum_{n\in\mathcal N_m(x)}\mathbf 1\{y_n=c\}
\] is the fraction of neighbors whose class is \(c\).


Answer

Each indicator \(\mathbf 1\{y_n=c\}\) equals \(1\) if neighbor \(n\) has class \(c\) and \(0\) otherwise. Summing over \(n\in\mathcal N_m(x)\) counts how many of the \(m\) neighbors have class \(c\). Dividing by \(m\) gives the fraction of neighbors in class \(c\).



27.0.13 Question 13
A nearest-neighbor classifier uses \(m=7\). Among the seven nearest neighbors of a query point, the class labels are \[
A,A,B,A,C,B,A.
\] Compute \(\hat s_{7,A}(x)\), \(\hat s_{7,B}(x)\), and \(\hat s_{7,C}(x)\), and give the predicted class.


Answer

The counts are \(4\) for class \(A\), \(2\) for class \(B\), and \(1\) for class \(C\). Therefore \[
\hat s_{7,A}(x)=\frac47,
\qquad
\hat s_{7,B}(x)=\frac27,
\qquad
\hat s_{7,C}(x)=\frac17.
\] The largest score is \(\hat s_{7,A}(x)\), so the predicted class is \(A\).



27.0.14 Question 14
A student claims: “Scaling cannot change nearest-neighbor predictions because scaling does not change the labels \(y_n\).” Diagnose the flaw in this claim.


Answer

The flaw is that nearest-neighbor predictions depend not only on labels but also on which points are selected as nearest neighbors. Scaling changes the distances between feature vectors, and therefore it can change the neighborhood set \(\mathcal N_m(x)\).
Even with the same labels \(y_n\), a different neighbor set can produce a different average response in regression or a different majority vote in classification.



27.0.15 Question 15
For nearest-neighbor regression, describe the qualitative behavior at the two extremes \(m=1\) and \(m=N\). Which one is more sensitive to individual training responses?


Answer

At \(m=1\), the prediction is the response of the single nearest training point. It is highly sensitive to individual training responses and can vary sharply as the nearest neighbor changes.
At \(m=N\), every prediction averages all training responses: \[
\hat s_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N y_n.
\] This ignores the query location entirely because every point has the same neighbor set. Thus \(m=1\) is most sensitive to individual responses, while \(m=N\) ignores \(x\) the most.

title: 28  Bias–Variance Tradeoff — Review Questions
text:

28.0.1 Question 1
In the lecture’s setup, \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}\) is random. Identify the source of this randomness and explain why \(f^*(x)\) is fixed.


Answer

The fitted predictor \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}=A(\mathcal D)\) is random because it is a function of the random training dataset \[
\mathcal D=\{(x_n,y_n)\}_{n=1}^N.
\] Different draws of \(\mathcal D\) can produce different fitted functions and therefore different values \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)\).
At a fixed input \(x\), \(f^*(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]\) is determined by the population distribution. It is not re-estimated for each training sample, so it is fixed in the pointwise decomposition.



28.0.2 Question 2
Starting from the model \(Y=f^*(X)+\varepsilon\), show that \[
(Y-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))^2 = (f^*(x)-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))^2+2\varepsilon(f^*(x)-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))+\varepsilon^2.
\]


Answer

At a fixed test input \(X=x\), the model gives \[
Y=f^*(x)+\varepsilon.
\] Therefore \[
(Y-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))^2=(f^*(x)+\varepsilon-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))^2.
\] Rearranging inside the square, \[
(f^*(x)-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)+\varepsilon)^2
=(f^*(x)-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))^2+2\varepsilon(f^*(x)-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))+\varepsilon^2.
\] These are the prediction-error term, the cross term, and the noise-squared term.



28.0.3 Question 3
Justify the step \[
\mathbb E[\varepsilon(f^*(x)-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))]=0.
\]


Answer

At test time, \(\varepsilon\) is the noise in the new response at \(X=x\), while \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)\) is determined by the training dataset \(\mathcal D\). We assume \[
\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X=x]=0
\] and that the new test observation is independent of the training data. Using conditional expectation,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E_{\mathcal D,\varepsilon\mid x}[\varepsilon(f^*(x)-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))]\\
&=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}\left[(f^*(x)-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))
\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X=x,\mathcal D]\right]=0.
\end{aligned}
\]



28.0.4 Question 4
Distinguish the variance term \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))\) from the noise variance \(\sigma^2\). What random quantity varies in each case?


Answer

The variance term \[
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))
\] measures how the fitted prediction at \(x\) changes across different random training datasets \(\mathcal D\).
The noise variance \[
\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X=x)
\] measures the randomness in the new response \(Y\) around the true signal \(f^*(x)\), even if the signal were known perfectly. The first is model instability; the second is irreducible output noise.



28.0.5 Question 5
Why is the noise term called irreducible error? Show that even if \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)=f^*(x)\), then \[
\mathbb E[(Y-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))^2 \mid X=x] = \sigma^2.
\]


Answer

If \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)=f^*(x)\) exactly, then squared prediction error at \(x\) is \[
(Y-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))^2=(f^*(x)+\varepsilon-f^*(x))^2=\varepsilon^2.
\] Taking expectation gives \[
\mathbb E[\varepsilon^2\mid X=x]=\sigma^2.
\] Thus even a perfect predictor of the true signal cannot remove the randomness in \(Y\) due to \(\varepsilon\). That is why \(\sigma^2\) is irreducible.



28.0.6 Question 6
A learning procedure has high bias but low variance at a point \(x\). Describe what repeated fitted models would look like at \(x\) relative to \(f^*(x)\).


Answer

Across repeated datasets, the fitted values \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)\) would be tightly clustered, because variance is low. However, the cluster would be centered far from \(f^*(x)\), because bias is high.
So the procedure is stable but systematically wrong at that point.



28.0.7 Question 7
At a fixed \(x\), suppose \[
\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)]=2.5,
\qquad
f^*(x)=3.0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))=0.16,
\qquad
\sigma^2=0.09.
\] Compute the squared bias and \(R(x)\).


Answer

The bias is \[
2.5-3.0=-0.5,
\] so the squared bias is \[
(-0.5)^2=0.25.
\] The risk is \[
R(x)=0.25+0.16+0.09=0.50.
\]



28.0.8 Question 8
The lecture says flexible models are often low-bias and high-variance. State this claim for nearest-neighbor regression by comparing small \(m\) and large \(m\).


Answer

With small \(m\), nearest-neighbor regression uses very local averages. This makes the fitted function flexible, so it can adapt to local structure in \(f^*\) and often has lower bias. But it also depends strongly on a small number of training points, so it has higher variance across datasets.
Large \(m\) averages many points. This stabilizes predictions and lowers variance, but it can smooth over local structure and increase bias.



28.0.9 Question 9
Why does increasing the sample size \(N\) often reduce variance? Explain why bias can nevertheless change as \(N\) increases.


Answer

Variance measures sensitivity to the random training dataset. With more data, a fitted predictor often becomes less sensitive to any particular observation, so variance tends to decrease.
Bias may remain similar when the model class and fitting behavior remain similar, but this is not guaranteed. The effective behavior of a procedure can change with \(N\). For example, in nearest-neighbor regression, more observations can make a neighborhood around \(x\) more local and reduce bias.



28.0.10 Question 10
Suppose \(\operatorname{Bias}(x)^2=0.36\), \(\operatorname{Var}(x)=0.04\), and \(\sigma^2=0.09\). If a richer model reduces squared bias to \(0.09\) but increases variance to \(0.20\), which model has lower pointwise risk at \(x\)?


Answer

The original model has risk \[
0.36+0.04+0.09=0.49.
\] The richer model has risk \[
0.09+0.20+0.09=0.38.
\] The richer model has lower pointwise risk at \(x\), despite its higher variance, because the reduction in squared bias is larger than the increase in variance.



28.0.11 Question 11
A student says: “Because variance is bad, we should always choose the lowest-variance model.” Diagnose the mistake using the decomposition from the lecture.


Answer

The mistake is ignoring squared bias. The pointwise risk is \[
R(x)=\operatorname{Bias}(x)^2+\operatorname{Var}(x)+\sigma^2.
\] A very low-variance procedure can still have high risk if its average prediction is far from \(f^*(x)\). The goal is to balance squared bias and variance, since the noise term is not controlled by the fitting procedure.



28.0.12 Question 12
Suppose the learning procedure always predicts \[
\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)=0
\] for every training dataset, while \[
f^*(x)=2.
\] Show that this procedure has zero variance but nonzero bias.


Answer

We then have: \[
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))=0
\] because the prediction never changes across datasets. But \[
\operatorname{Bias}(x)=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)]-f^*(x)=0-2=-2,
\] so the squared bias is \(4\).



28.0.13 Question 13
Does the lecture’s displayed identity—squared bias plus variance plus noise—hold unchanged for 0-1 loss or absolute-error loss?


Answer

No. The derivation relies on expanding a square: \[
(Y-\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x))^2.
\] This expansion produces terms that can be identified as squared bias, variance, and noise, with cross terms that vanish under the stated assumptions.
For absolute error or 0-1 loss, there is no analogous simple quadratic expansion into these exact three terms. Other decompositions can be defined, and the bias–variance idea remains useful qualitatively, but this displayed identity is specific to squared-error regression.



28.0.14 Question 14
At a point \(x\), three procedures have the following squared bias and variance, with common \(\sigma^2=0.1\):



procedure
squared bias
variance




A
0.50
0.05


B
0.20
0.20


C
0.05
0.60



Compute the risk for each procedure and identify the best one at this \(x\).


Answer

Procedure A has risk \[
0.50+0.05+0.10=0.65.
\] Procedure B has risk \[
0.20+0.20+0.10=0.50.
\] Procedure C has risk \[
0.05+0.60+0.10=0.75.
\] Procedure B is best at this \(x\) because it has the smallest total risk.



28.0.15 Question 15
A false proof says: “The cross term vanishes because \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)-f^*(x)]=0\).” Identify why this proof is wrong in general.


Answer

The statement \[
\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)-f^*(x)]=0
\] means the estimator is unbiased at \(x\). The lecture does not assume unbiasedness; in fact, bias may be nonzero and is one of the terms being measured.
The first cross term involving \(\varepsilon\) vanishes because the test noise has conditional mean zero and the test observation is independent of \(\mathcal D\). The second cross term vanishes because \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)-\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)]\) is centered, not because \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(x)-f^*(x)\) is centered.



28.0.16 Question 16
Suppose the irreducible noise variance is \(\sigma^2=1\). At a fixed test point \(x_0\), two prediction procedures have the following bias and variance:



Procedure
Bias\(^2\)
Variance




A
\(0\)
\(4\)


B
\(3\)
\(1\)



Using the bias–variance decomposition, show that the two procedures have the same pointwise risk at \(x_0\), but different bias–variance behavior.


Answer

For Procedure A, the risk is
\[
0+4+1=5.
\]
So Procedure A has total risk \(5\).
For Procedure B, the risk is
\[
3+1+1=5.
\]
So Procedure B also has total risk \(5\).
Therefore, the two procedures have the same pointwise risk at \(x_0\), even though the source of the error is different.

title: 29  Ridge Regression - Review Questions
text:
Warning: AI-assisted materials These materials were developed with assistance from AI tools. All content has been reviewed and edited by the instructor, who takes final responsibility for its accuracy, clarity, and appropriateness for the course. Students should treat these materials as instructor-reviewed course content while applying the same critical judgment they would use with any technical material. Please report any suspected errors or unclear explanations to ghunt@wm.edu.


29.0.1 Question 1
The lecture describes ridge regression as an example of regularization. How does this regularization work for ridge, what quantity controls the strength of regularization, and what happens at the two extremes \(\lambda=0\) and \(\lambda\to\infty\)?


Answer

Ridge regularizes the coefficient vector \(w\) by adding the penalty \[
\lambda\|w\|_2^2
\] to the squared-error training objective. The regularization strength is controlled by \(\lambda\ge0\).
At \(\lambda=0\), the penalty disappears and the problem reduces to OLS. As \(\lambda\to\infty\), any nonzero penalized coefficient becomes extremely costly, so the fitted slopes are driven toward \(0\). An unpenalized intercept need not approach zero.



29.0.2 Question 2
For \(w=(3,-4,12)\), compute \(\|w\|_2^2\). If \(\lambda=0.5\), what is the ridge penalty value \(\lambda\|w\|_2^2\)?


Answer

The squared norm is \[
\|w\|_2^2=3^2+(-4)^2+12^2=9+16+144=169.
\] Thus the penalty value is \[
\lambda\|w\|_2^2=0.5(169)=84.5.
\]



29.0.3 Question 3
Why does minimizing training error alone fail to control model complexity? How does ridge control model complexity?


Answer

Training error can be reduced by increasing flexibility, but greater flexibility can fit noise and sample-specific patterns. For example, in polynomial regression, increasing degree can keep lowering training error while eventually increasing test error. In nearest-neighbor regression, very small \(m\) gives highly local fits that can have high variance.
Ridge addresses the same issue for linear regression by keeping the model class linear but penalizing large coefficients. The penalty discourages overly flexible or unstable coefficient choices even if they improve training error.



29.0.4 Question 4
Starting from the unnormalized ridge objective used in the solving section, \[
J_\lambda(w)=\|y-Xw\|_2^2+\lambda\|w\|_2^2,
\] expand \(J_\lambda(w)\) into quadratic form involving \(y^\top y\), \(w^\top X^\top y\), \(w^\top X^\top Xw\), and \(w^\top w\).


Answer

First, \[
\|y-Xw\|_2^2=(y-Xw)^\top(y-Xw).
\] Expanding gives \[
y^\top y-y^\top Xw-w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw.
\] Since \(y^\top Xw\) is a scalar equal to \(w^\top X^\top y\), this becomes \[
y^\top y-2w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw.
\] Adding the penalty gives \[
J_\lambda(w)=y^\top y-2w^\top X^\top y+w^\top X^\top Xw+
\lambda w^\top w.
\]



29.0.5 Question 5
Differentiate the expanded objective from Question 4 and derive the ridge normal equations.


Answer

Using the standard rules, \[
\nabla_w(y^\top y)=0,
\qquad
\nabla_w(w^\top X^\top y)=X^\top y,
\] \[
\nabla_w(w^\top X^\top Xw)=2X^\top Xw,
\qquad
\nabla_w(w^\top w)=2w.
\] Therefore \[
\nabla_wJ_\lambda(w)=2X^\top Xw-2X^\top y+2\lambda w.
\] Setting this equal to zero and dividing by \(2\) gives \[
X^\top Xw-X^\top y+
\lambda w=0.
\] Thus \[
(X^\top X+
\lambda I_D)w=X^\top y.
\]



29.0.6 Question 6
In the scalar case \(D=1\), let \(X^\top X=9\), \(X^\top y=18\), and \(\lambda=3\) under the unnormalized convention. Compute the OLS coefficient and the ridge coefficient.


Answer

The OLS coefficient is \[
\widehat w_{\mathrm{OLS}}=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y=\frac{18}{9}=2.
\] The ridge coefficient is \[
\widehat w_\lambda=(X^\top X+
\lambda)^{-1}X^\top y=\frac{18}{9+3}=\frac{18}{12}=1.5.
\] Ridge shrinks the coefficient toward zero.



29.0.7 Question 7
Why does ridge regression stabilize solutions when features are highly correlated? Give a precise explanation using the lecture’s example where \(X_{:2}\approx X_{:1}\).


Answer

If \(X_{:2}\approx X_{:1}\), then \[
w_1X_{:1}+w_2X_{:2}\approx (w_1+w_2)X_{:1}.
\] Many pairs \((w_1,w_2)\) with similar sums can produce nearly the same predictions. OLS may therefore choose large cancelling coefficients, such as \((100,-99)\), with little change in training error.
Ridge penalizes \[
w_1^2+w_2^2,
\] so large cancelling coefficients become costly. Among coefficient vectors with similar fit, ridge prefers smaller Euclidean norm, producing a more stable solution.



29.0.8 Question 8
The lecture states that ridge replaces \(X^\top X\) with \(X^\top X+\lambda I_D\), which is invertible when \(\lambda>0\). Suppose \(X^\top Xv=\sigma^2v\) for a nonzero vector \(v\). Show that \(v\) is also an eigenvector of \(X^\top X+\lambda I_D\), identify its new eigenvalue, and explain why this supports the invertibility claim.


Answer

Compute \[
(X^\top X+\lambda I_D)v=X^\top Xv+\lambda I_Dv.
\] Using \(X^\top Xv=\sigma^2v\) and \(I_Dv=v\), \[
(X^\top X+\lambda I_D)v=\sigma^2v+\lambda v=(\sigma^2+\lambda)v.
\] Thus \(v\) remains an eigenvector, and the new eigenvalue is \(\sigma^2+\lambda\). Because \(X^\top X\) has nonnegative eigenvalues, \(\sigma^2+\lambda>0\) whenever \(\lambda>0\). The ridge matrix therefore has no zero eigenvalues and is invertible.



29.0.9 Question 9
For orthonormal predictors satisfying \(X^\top X=I_D\), derive the ridge estimator and express it in terms of the OLS estimator.


Answer

The ridge estimator is \[
\widehat w_\lambda=(X^\top X+
\lambda I_D)^{-1}X^\top y.
\] Using \(X^\top X=I_D\), \[
\widehat w_\lambda=(I_D+
\lambda I_D)^{-1}X^\top y=((1+
\lambda)I_D)^{-1}X^\top y.
\] Therefore \[
\widehat w_\lambda=\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}X^\top y.
\] Since \(\widehat w_{\mathrm{OLS}}=X^\top y\) in this case, \[
\widehat w_\lambda=\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}\widehat w_{\mathrm{OLS}}.
\]



29.0.10 Question 10
In an orthonormal-design problem, suppose \(\widehat w_{\mathrm{OLS}}=(4,-2,1)\) and \(\lambda=3\). Compute \(\widehat w_\lambda\).


Answer

The shrinkage factor is \[
\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}=\frac14.
\] Therefore \[
\widehat w_\lambda=\frac14(4,-2,1)=\left(1,-\frac12,\frac14\right).
\]



29.0.11 Question 11
The lecture recommends standardizing predictors before ridge regression. Why is this necessary for the penalty \(\lambda\sum_jw_j^2\) to treat predictors comparably?


Answer

Coefficient size depends on feature units. If one predictor is measured in thousands and another in units near one, the same predictive effect can require very different coefficient magnitudes. Since ridge penalizes coefficient magnitudes directly, \[
\lambda\sum_jw_j^2,
\] the penalty depends on the measurement scale of each feature.
Standardizing features to comparable scales, usually mean zero and variance one, makes coefficient sizes more comparable. Then the penalty is less distorted by arbitrary units.



29.0.12 Question 12
State the penalized and constrained forms of ridge regression.


Answer

The penalized form is \[
\min_w \|y-Xw\|_2^2+\lambda\|w\|_2^2.
\] The constrained form is \[
\min_w \|y-Xw\|_2^2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \|w\|_2^2\le t.
\]



29.0.13 Question 13
For a diagonal design with \[
X^\top X=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
X^\top y=\begin{pmatrix}8\\3\end{pmatrix},
\] compute the ridge solution for \(\lambda=1\).


Answer

The ridge system is \[
(X^\top X+
\lambda I)w=X^\top y.
\] With \(\lambda=1\), \[
X^\top X+
I=
\begin{pmatrix}5&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\] Therefore \[
w=\begin{pmatrix}5^{-1}&0\\0&2^{-1}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}8\\3\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}8/5\\3/2\end{pmatrix}.
\] So \[
\hat w_\lambda=(1.6,1.5)^\top.
\]



29.0.14 Question 14
How does increasing \(\lambda\) affect the bias-variance tradeoff in ridge regression? Give the expected direction of training error and test error for very small versus moderate \(\lambda\).


Answer

Increasing \(\lambda\) shrinks coefficients and reduces model flexibility. This usually increases bias but lowers variance.
For very small \(\lambda\), ridge is close to OLS: training error is low, but variance may be high and test error can be poor in noisy, collinear, or high-dimensional settings. For moderate \(\lambda\), training error may increase, but test error can decrease because the reduction in variance and instability outweighs the increase in bias. For very large \(\lambda\), underfitting can make test error increase again.



29.0.15 Question 15
The riboflavin example has \(D>N\). Why can OLS have multiple coefficient solutions in this setting, and how does ridge with \(\lambda>0\) resolve that ambiguity?


Answer

When \(D>N\), the \(D\) columns of \(X\) cannot all be linearly independent. Consequently, there is a nonzero vector \(z\) such that \(Xz=0\). If \(w\) is an OLS solution, then \(w+z\) gives the same fitted values because \[
X(w+z)=Xw+Xz=Xw.
\] Thus the training error may not determine a unique coefficient vector.
Ridge adds the penalty \(\lambda\|w\|_2^2\), favoring smaller coefficient vectors among solutions with similar fit. For \(\lambda>0\), its normal equations use \[
X^\top X+\lambda I_D,
\] which is invertible, so ridge has a unique coefficient solution.

title: 30  LASSO - Review Questions
text:
Warning: AI-assisted materials These materials were developed with assistance from AI tools. All content has been reviewed and edited by the instructor, who takes final responsibility for its accuracy, clarity, and appropriateness for the course. Students should treat these materials as instructor-reviewed course content while applying the same critical judgment they would use with any technical material. Please report any suspected errors or unclear explanations to ghunt@wm.edu.


30.0.1 Question 1
LASSO stands for least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. Why?


Answer

The penalty \[
\lambda\|w\|_1=\lambda\sum_j |w_j|
\] causes shrinkage because it makes large coefficient magnitudes costly, pulling estimates toward zero.
Selection occurs because the \(\ell_1\) penalty can set some coefficients exactly equal to zero. A coefficient with \(\widehat w_j=0\) effectively removes predictor \(j\) from the fitted linear model. This selects out the corresponding variable.



30.0.2 Question 2
For \(w=(3,-1,0,2)\), compute \(\|w\|_1\), \(\|w\|_2^2\), and the number of “selected” variables.


Answer

The \(\ell_1\) norm is \[
\|w\|_1=|3|+|-1|+|0|+|2|=6.
\] The squared \(\ell_2\) norm is \[
\|w\|_2^2=3^2+(-1)^2+0^2+2^2=14.
\] There are three nonzero coefficients, so the number of selected variables is \(3\).



30.0.3 Question 3
What is the main optimization hurdle for LASSO as compared to ridge?


Answer

Ridge uses the smooth squared \(\ell_2\) penalty \(\|w\|_2^2\), so the objective is differentiable and leads to normal equations with a closed-form matrix solution.
LASSO uses the \(\ell_1\) penalty \(\|w\|_1=\sum_j |w_j|\). The absolute value is not differentiable at zero, so the objective is convex but nonsmooth. Because of this nonsmoothness, LASSO generally does not have a simple closed-form matrix formula like ridge.



30.0.4 Question 4
State the subdifferential of \(|u|\) at \(u>0\), \(u=0\), and \(u<0\).


Answer

The subdifferential is \[
\partial |u|=\begin{cases}
\{1\},&u>0,\\
[-1,1],&u=0,\\
\{-1\},&u<0.
\end{cases}
\] At zero, the subdifferential is an entire interval rather than a single slope.



30.0.5 Question 5
In coordinate descent, the partial residual for coordinate \(j\) is \[
r_j=y-\sum_{\ell\ne j}X_{:\ell}w_\ell.
\] Show that if \(\widehat y=Xw=\sum_{\ell=1}^D X_{:\ell}w_\ell\), then \[
r_j=y-\widehat y+X_{:j}w_j.
\]


Answer

Since \[
\widehat y=\sum_{\ell=1}^D X_{:\ell}w_\ell=X_{:j}w_j+\sum_{\ell\ne j}X_{:\ell}w_\ell,
\] we have \[
\sum_{\ell\ne j}X_{:\ell}w_\ell=\widehat y-X_{:j}w_j.
\] Substitute into the definition of \(r_j\): \[
r_j=y-(\widehat y-X_{:j}w_j)=y-\widehat y+X_{:j}w_j.
\]



30.0.6 Question 6
In the coordinate-descent derivation, \(z_j=(1/N)X_{:j}^\top r_j\). Give an interpretation of \(z_j\).


Answer

The value \[
z_j=\frac1N X_{:j}^\top r_j
\] measures the empirical alignment, or covariance-like relationship, between feature \(j\) and the remaining residual. If \(|z_j|\) is large, feature \(j\) explains residual variation not already explained by the other variables.



30.0.7 Question 7
Starting from \[
\frac{1}{2N}\|r_j-X_{:j}w_j\|_2^2+
\lambda|w_j|,
\] expand the terms that depend on \(w_j\) and derive \[
g_j(w_j)=\frac12a_jw_j^2-z_jw_j+
\lambda|w_j|,
\] where \(a_j=(1/N)X_{:j}^\top X_{:j}\) and \(z_j=(1/N)X_{:j}^\top r_j\). You can drop any term that doesn’t depend on \(w_j\).


Answer

Expand the squared term: \[
\frac{1}{2N}(r_j-X_{:j}w_j)^\top(r_j-X_{:j}w_j)
=
\frac{1}{2N}\left(r_j^\top r_j-2w_jX_{:j}^\top r_j+w_j^2X_{:j}^\top X_{:j}\right).
\] The term \((1/(2N))r_j^\top r_j\) does not depend on \(w_j\), so it can be dropped for minimization. The remaining terms are \[
-\frac1N w_jX_{:j}^\top r_j+
\frac12\frac1N X_{:j}^\top X_{:j} w_j^2+
\lambda|w_j|.
\] Using \(a_j=(1/N)X_{:j}^\top X_{:j}\) and \(z_j=(1/N)X_{:j}^\top r_j\) gives \[
g_j(w_j)=\frac12a_jw_j^2-z_jw_j+
\lambda|w_j|.
\]



30.0.8 Question 8
For the coordinate objective \[
g_j(w_j)=\frac12a_jw_j^2-z_jw_j+
\lambda|w_j|,
\] derive the subdifferential.


Answer

The differentiable part is \[
\frac12a_jw_j^2-z_jw_j,
\] whose derivative is \[
a_jw_j-z_j.
\] The nonsmooth part is \(\lambda|w_j|\), whose subdifferential is \[
\lambda\partial|w_j|.
\] Adding the derivative of the smooth part and the subdifferential of the nonsmooth part gives \[
\partial g_j(w_j)=a_jw_j-z_j+
\lambda\partial|w_j|.
\]



30.0.9 Question 9
At \(w_j=0\), show that \[
\partial g_j(0)=[-z_j-\lambda,
-z_j+
\lambda].
\] Then state the condition on \(z_j\) under which \(w_j=0\) satisfies the optimality condition.


Answer

At \(w_j=0\), \[
a_jw_j-z_j=-z_j.
\] Also, \[
\partial|0|=[-1,1].
\] Therefore \[
\partial g_j(0)=-z_j+
\lambda[-1,1]=[-z_j-
\lambda,-z_j+
\lambda].
\] The optimality condition is \(0\in\partial g_j(0)\). This holds exactly when \[
-z_j-
\lambda\le0\le -z_j+
\lambda,
\] which is equivalent to \[
|z_j|\le\lambda.
\]



30.0.10 Question 10
Derive the positive-coordinate case of the LASSO update: if \(z_j>\lambda\), show that the minimizer satisfies
\[
w_j=\frac{z_j-\lambda}{a_j}.
\]


Answer

The coordinate-wise objective has subdifferential
\[
\partial g_j(w_j)=a_jw_j-z_j+\lambda \partial |w_j|.
\]
A value of \(w_j\) is optimal exactly when
\[
0 \in \partial g_j(w_j).
\]
Assume \(z_j>\lambda\). First check whether \(w_j=0\) can be optimal. At \(w_j=0\),
\[
\partial g_j(0)=[-z_j-\lambda,-z_j+\lambda].
\]
Since \(z_j>\lambda\), the upper endpoint satisfies \(-z_j+\lambda<0\). Therefore this whole interval is negative, so \(0\notin\partial g_j(0)\). Thus \(w_j=0\) is not optimal.
Now check whether a negative value can be optimal. If \(w_j<0\), then \(\partial |w_j|=\{-1\}\), so
\[
\partial g_j(w_j)=\{a_jw_j-z_j-\lambda\}.
\]
Since \(a_j>0\) and \(w_j<0\), we have \(a_jw_j<0\). Also, \(z_j>\lambda>0\). Therefore \(a_jw_j-z_j-\lambda<0\), so the subdifferential cannot contain zero for any \(w_j<0\).
So the minimizer must be positive. For \(w_j>0\), \(\partial |w_j|=\{1\}\), so
\[
\partial g_j(w_j)=\{a_jw_j-z_j+\lambda\}.
\]
To make zero belong to this set, solve
\[
a_jw_j-z_j+\lambda=0.
\]
This gives
\[
w_j=\frac{z_j-\lambda}{a_j}.
\]
Because \(z_j>\lambda\) and \(a_j>0\), this value is positive. Therefore it is consistent with the positive case and satisfies the subgradient optimality condition. Since \(g_j\) is convex, it is the minimizer.



30.0.11 Question 11
Compute \(S(z,\lambda)\) for \(\lambda=0.5\) and \[
z\in\{-1.2,-0.5,-0.1,0.7,2.0\}.
\]


Answer

Using soft-thresholding:

\(S(-1.2,0.5)=-1.2+0.5=-0.7\).
\(S(-0.5,0.5)=0\) because \(|z|\le\lambda\).
\(S(-0.1,0.5)=0\) because \(|z|\le\lambda\).
\(S(0.7,0.5)=0.7-0.5=0.2\).
\(S(2.0,0.5)=2.0-0.5=1.5\).




30.0.12 Question 12
A coordinate has \(a_j=2\), \(z_j=-3\), and \(\lambda=1\). Compute the coordinate descent update for \(w_j\).


Answer

Since \[
z_j=-3<-
\lambda=-1,
\] use the negative case: \[
w_j\leftarrow\frac{z_j+
\lambda}{a_j}=\frac{-3+1}{2}=-1.
\]



30.0.13 Question 13
Compare ridge and LASSO in the orthonormal-predictor case under the normalized-loss convention used in the LASSO lecture. If \(z_j\) is the OLS coefficient, what does ridge do to \(z_j\), and what does LASSO do to \(z_j\)?


Answer

In the orthonormal case, ridge rescales every coefficient by the same factor: \[
\widehat w_{\lambda,j}^{\mathrm{ridge}}=\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}z_j
\] under this convention.
LASSO applies soft-thresholding: \[
\widehat w_{\lambda,j}^{\mathrm{LASSO}}=S(z_j,\lambda)=\operatorname{sign}(z_j)(|z_j|-
\lambda)_+.
\] Thus ridge continuously shrinks all coefficients, while LASSO sets coefficients to zero when \(|z_j|\le\lambda\) and shrinks the rest by subtracting \(\lambda\) from their magnitude.



30.0.14 Question 14
For orthonormal predictors, let \(z=(2.0,0.4,-1.5)\) and \(\lambda=1\). Compute the LASSO solution and the ridge solution using the shrinkage factor \(1/(1+
\lambda)\).


Answer

For LASSO, \[
S(2.0,1)=1.0,
\qquad
S(0.4,1)=0,
\qquad
S(-1.5,1)=-0.5.
\] So \[
\widehat w_\lambda^{\mathrm{LASSO}}=(1.0,0,-0.5).
\] For ridge, the shrinkage factor is \[
\frac{1}{1+
\lambda}=\frac12.
\] Thus \[
\widehat w_\lambda^{\mathrm{ridge}}=(1.0,0.2,-0.75).
\]



30.0.15 Question 15
In two dimensions, describe the set \[
\{(w_1,w_2): |w_1|+|w_2|\le 1\}.
\] List its four vertices.


Answer

The set is the two-dimensional \(\ell_1\) unit ball, which is a diamond. Its boundary consists of the lines \[
|w_1|+|w_2|=1.
\] The four vertices are \[
(1,0),
\quad
(0,1),
\quad
(-1,0),
\quad
(0,-1).
\] These vertices lie on the coordinate axes.



30.0.16 Question 16
Use the geometry from the lecture to explain why LASSO can produce exact zeros while ridge usually does not.


Answer

In the constrained view, ridge uses a round \(\ell_2\) ball, while LASSO uses a diamond-shaped \(\ell_1\) ball. The LASSO diamond has corners on the coordinate axes.
The solution is where the smallest attainable loss contour touches the constraint region. Because the \(\ell_1\) ball has corners on the axes, tangency often occurs at a point where one or more coordinates are exactly zero. The ridge ball is smooth and round, so tangency is less likely to occur exactly on an axis; ridge usually shrinks coefficients without setting them exactly to zero.



30.0.17 Question 17
For coefficient vectors \(u=(1,1)\) and \(v=(2,0)\), compare their \(\ell_1\) and squared \(\ell_2\) penalties. Use this to explain why LASSO may be indifferent between spreading and concentrating coefficients in some correlated-feature settings.


Answer

For \(u=(1,1)\), \[
\|u\|_1=2,
\qquad
\|u\|_2^2=1^2+1^2=2.
\] For \(v=(2,0)\), \[
\|v\|_1=2,
\qquad
\|v\|_2^2=2^2+0^2=4.
\] The two vectors have the same \(\ell_1\) norm but different squared \(\ell_2\) norms. This shows that an \(\ell_1\) penalty may not strongly prefer spreading weight across correlated variables, while ridge’s squared \(\ell_2\) penalty favors spreading because it penalizes concentration more heavily.



30.0.18 Question 18
Describe the typical qualitative relationship between \(\lambda\) and selected model complexity.


Answer

As \(\lambda\) increases, the number of nonzero coefficients generally tends to decrease. Larger \(\lambda\) imposes stronger \(\ell_1\) regularization, so more coefficients tend to fail the soft-thresholding condition and become zero.
Thus selected model complexity, measured by the number of nonzero coefficients, typically decreases as \(\lambda\) increases. The active-set size need not change monotonically in every dataset, especially when predictors are correlated.



30.0.19 Question 19
Why should predictors be standardized before applying LASSO?


Answer

LASSO penalizes coefficient magnitudes through \[
\lambda\sum_j |w_j|.
\] Coefficient magnitude depends on feature units. If one predictor is measured in thousands, a small coefficient can have a large predictive effect. If another predictor is measured in tiny units, the same predictive effect may require a large coefficient.
Without standardization, LASSO may penalize the small-scale variable more heavily simply because its coefficient must be numerically larger. Standardizing puts predictors on comparable scales so the penalty treats them more fairly.

title: 31  Feed-Forward Neural Networks - Review Questions
text:
Warning: AI-assisted materials These materials were developed with assistance from AI tools. All content has been reviewed and edited by the instructor, who takes final responsibility for its accuracy, clarity, and appropriateness for the course. Students should treat these materials as instructor-reviewed course content while applying the same critical judgment they would use with any technical material. Please report any suspected errors or unclear explanations to ghunt@wm.edu.


31.0.1 Question 1
A network has layer sizes \[
[3,4,3,1].
\] I.e. it has a 3-vector input and outputs a single number. Using the lecture’s formula, compute the number of parameters in each layer and the total number of parameters.


Answer

For a layer mapping width \(d_{i-1}\) to width \(d_i\), the number of parameters is \[
d_id_{i-1}+d_i.
\] For \(3\to4\): \[
4\cdot3+4=16.
\] For \(4\to3\): \[
3\cdot4+3=15.
\] For \(3\to1\): \[
1\cdot3+1=4.
\] The total is \[
16+15+4=35.
\]



31.0.2 Question 2
The lecture contrasts feature engineering and feature learning. What’s the difference?


Answer

Feature engineering manually constructs new inputs before fitting a model. For example, one could replace \(x=(x_1,x_2)\) by \[
(x_1,x_2,x_1^2,x_2^2,x_1x_2)
\] and then fit a linear model in this expanded representation.
Feature learning lets the model learn intermediate features from data. In a neural network, the first hidden layer might compute \[
h^{(1)}=\phi(W^{(1)}x+b^{(1)}),
\] so the learned features are the coordinates of \(h^{(1)}\) rather than manually specified polynomial terms.



31.0.3 Question 3
Suppose layer \(i\) has input dimension \(d_{i-1}=5\) and output dimension \(d_i=7\). State the dimensions of \(W^{(i)}\), \(b^{(i)}\), \(W^{(i)}h+b^{(i)}\), and \(s_i(h)\).


Answer

The weight matrix has shape \[
W^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^{7\times5}.
\] The bias vector has shape \[
b^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^7.
\] For \(h\in\mathbb R^5\), \[
W^{(i)}h\in\mathbb R^7,
\] so \[
W^{(i)}h+b^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^7.
\] Because \(\phi_i\) maps \(\mathbb R^7\) to \(\mathbb R^7\) componentwise, \[
s_i(h)=\phi_i(W^{(i)}h+b^{(i)})\in\mathbb R^7.
\]



31.0.4 Question 4
A one-hidden-layer regression network has input dimension \(D=10\), \(H=6\) hidden units, and a single output dimension. It uses \[
h=\phi(Wx+b),\qquad s_\theta(x)=v^\top h+b^{\mathrm{out}}.
\] Compute the total number of parameters.


Answer

The hidden layer has \[
W\in\mathbb R^{6\times10}
\] with \(60\) weights and \[
b\in\mathbb R^6
\] with \(6\) biases. That is \(66\) hidden-layer parameters.
The output layer has \[
v\in\mathbb R^6
\] with \(6\) weights and scalar bias \(b^{\mathrm{out}}\), giving \(7\) output-layer parameters.
The total is \[
66+7=73.
\]



31.0.5 Question 5
Why are nonlinear activation functions essential if we want a multilayer network to represent more than a linear model?


Answer

If every activation is the identity, then each layer is just an affine transformation. A composition of affine transformations is itself affine. Therefore, even a deep network with only identity activations collapses to a single affine score function. Nonlinear activations such as ReLU, sigmoid, or tanh prevent this collapse. They allow the network to build nonlinear transformations of the input and become more flexible than a linear model.



31.0.6 Question 6
Prove that a two-layer network with identity activations is affine. Specifically, let \[
h=W^{(1)}x+b^{(1)},
\qquad
s(x)=W^{(2)}h+b^{(2)}.
\] Write \(s(x)\) as a single affine function of \(x\): \[
s(x)=Ax+a.
\]


Answer

Substitute the first layer into the second: \[
s(x)=W^{(2)}(W^{(1)}x+b^{(1)})+b^{(2)}.
\] Distribute: \[
s(x)=W^{(2)}W^{(1)}x+W^{(2)}b^{(1)}+b^{(2)}.
\] This has the form \[
s(x)=Ax+a,
\] where \[
A=W^{(2)}W^{(1)},
\qquad
a=W^{(2)}b^{(1)}+b^{(2)}.
\] Thus the two-layer identity-activation network is just one affine map.



31.0.7 Question 7
What does it mean for a network to be feed-forward?


Answer

Feed-forward means information moves in one direction through the network. The input \(x\) is transformed into the first hidden representation \(h^{(1)}\), then into \(h^{(2)}\), and so on until the output score \(s_\theta(x)\) is produced. There are no feedback loops in this description: later layers do not feed their outputs back into earlier layers. Each layer receives input from the previous layer and passes its output forward.



31.0.8 Question 8
For a classification network with a single hidden width \(H=8\) and \(K=3\) classes, the final affine layer has \[
s_\theta(x)=Vh+b^{\mathrm{out}}.
\] State the dimensions of \(V\), \(b^{\mathrm{out}}\), and \(s_\theta(x)\).


Answer

The hidden representation satisfies \[
h\in\mathbb R^8.
\] To produce \(K=3\) logits, \[
V\in\mathbb R^{3\times8},
\qquad
b^{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb R^3.
\] Then \[
Vh+b^{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb R^3.
\] Thus \[
s_\theta(x)\in\mathbb R^3.
\]



31.0.9 Question 9
The lecture says classification network outputs are often treated as logits. What is a logit in this context, and why are logits not probabilities?


Answer

A logit is a raw class score produced by the final affine layer of the network. For \(K\) classes, the logit vector is \[
s_\theta(x)\in\mathbb R^K.
\] Logits are not probabilities because their entries can be negative, positive, or zero, and they do not have to sum to one. To obtain probabilities, one applies the softmax function: \[
p_\theta(x)=\operatorname{softmax}(s_\theta(x)).
\]



31.0.10 Question 10
A classifier has logits \[
s=(0,\log 2,\log 3).
\] Compute the softmax probability vector.


Answer

Softmax probabilities are \[
p_c=\frac{e^{s_c}}{\sum_{r=1}^K e^{s_r}}.
\] Here \[
e^0=1,
\qquad
e^{\log2}=2,
\qquad
e^{\log3}=3.
\] The denominator is \(1+2+3=6\). Therefore \[
p=\left(\frac16,\frac26,\frac36\right)=\left(\frac16,\frac13,\frac12\right).
\]



31.0.11 Question 11
A network architecture has \(D=20\) inputs, hidden widths \[
\quad d_1=10,
\quad d_2=5,
\] and outputs \(K=4\) logits. Compute the total number of parameters.


Answer

The \(20\to10\) layer has \[
10\cdot20+10=210
\] parameters.
The \(10\to5\) layer has \[
5\cdot10+5=55
\] parameters.
The \(5\to4\) layer has \[
4\cdot5+4=24
\] parameters.
The total is \[
210+55+24=289.
\]



31.0.12 Question 12
For one-hidden-layer classification, \[
h=\phi(Wx+b),\qquad s_\theta(x)=Vh+b^{\mathrm{out}},
\] with \(K\) classes and \(H\) hidden units. Derive the shapes of \(W\), \(b\), \(V\), and \(b^{\mathrm{out}}\) when \(x\in\mathbb R^D\).


Answer

The hidden layer maps \(\mathbb R^D\) to \(\mathbb R^H\), so \[
W\in\mathbb R^{H\times D},
\qquad
b\in\mathbb R^H.
\] Then \[
h=\phi(Wx+b)\in\mathbb R^H.
\] The output layer maps \(\mathbb R^H\) to \(\mathbb R^K\), so \[
V\in\mathbb R^{K\times H},
\qquad
b^{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb R^K.
\] Thus \[
s_\theta(x)=Vh+b^{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb R^K.
\]



31.0.13 Question 13
For predicted class probabilities \[
p=(0.1,0.7,0.2)
\] and true class \(y=2\), compute the categorical cross-entropy loss. Use natural logarithms.


Answer

The correct-class probability is \[
p_y=p_2=0.7.
\] The loss is \[
-\log(p_y)=-\log(0.7)\approx 0.357.
\]



31.0.14 Question 14
Suppose a hidden layer uses ReLU activation, \(\phi(t)=\max\{0,t\}\) componentwise. For pre-activation vector \[
a=(-2,0,3),
\] compute the hidden representation \(h=\phi(a)\).


Answer

Apply ReLU to each coordinate: \[
\phi(-2)=0,
\qquad
\phi(0)=0,
\qquad
\phi(3)=3.
\] Thus \[
h=(0,0,3).
\]



31.0.15 Question 15
A hidden layer maps \(\mathbb R^4\) to \(\mathbb R^3\) using an affine map and an activation. How many weights and biases does this layer have?


Answer

Here \(d_{i-1}=4\) and \(d_i=3\). The weight matrix has \[
3\cdot4=12
\] entries. The bias vector has \[
3
\] entries. The layer has \[
12+3=15
\] parameters.



31.0.16 Question 16
For a classification network with logits \[
s=(2,1,0),
\] Which class is predicted? Does applying softmax change the predicted class?


Answer

The largest logit is the first entry, \(2\), so the predicted class is class \(1\) if classes are indexed as \(1,2,3\). Applying softmax does not change the predicted class because softmax is monotone in each logit relative to the others: the largest logit gets the largest softmax probability.



31.0.17 Question 17
Why does the lecture describe neural networks as learning intermediate representations?


Answer

Each hidden layer produces a new representation of the input, such as \[
h^{(1)}=s_1(x),
\qquad
h^{(2)}=s_2(h^{(1)}).
\] These representations are not fixed before training; they depend on learned weights and biases. The final layer then makes predictions from the last learned representation.
Thus the network learns both the features and the final prediction rule, rather than fitting a linear model to a fixed feature representation supplied in advance.

Students should treat these materials as instructor-reviewed course content while applying the same critical judgment they would use with any technical material. Please report any suspected errors or unclear explanations to ghunt@wm.edu.


32.0.1 Question 1
State what remains the same and what changes when the lecture moves from linear/logistic regression to neural-network training. Your answer should mention the empirical risk, the score function, and the optimization problem.


Answer

The ERM structure is unchanged: choose a score function, choose a loss, and minimize
\[
\hat R(\theta)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N \ell(y_n,s_\theta(x_n)).
\]
What changes is the score class. Instead of a linear score, the model uses a layered composition
\[
s_\theta(x)=s_L(s_{L-1}(\cdots s_1(x)\cdots)),
\]
with many parameters across layers. The resulting optimization problem is usually nonconvex and generally has no closed-form solution, so gradient-based iterative methods are used.



32.0.2 Question 2
For the one-hidden-unit model
\[
a_n=wx_n+b,\qquad h_n=\sigma(a_n),\qquad s_n=vh_n+c,
\]
with empirical risk
\[
\hat{R}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \frac{1}{2}(y_n-s_n)^2
\]
derive the gradients
\[
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial v},\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial c},\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial w},\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial b}
\]
using the chain rule.
Hint: Work first with one observation,
\[
\ell_n=\frac{1}{2}(y_n-s_n)^2.
\]
Use the paths
\[
\ell_n \to s_n \to v,\qquad
\ell_n \to s_n \to c,\qquad
\ell_n \to s_n \to h_n \to a_n \to w,\qquad
\ell_n \to s_n \to h_n \to a_n \to b.
\]
Compute the intermediate derivatives
\[
\frac{\partial \ell_n}{\partial s_n},\quad
\frac{\partial s_n}{\partial v},\quad
\frac{\partial s_n}{\partial c},\quad
\frac{\partial s_n}{\partial h_n},\quad
\frac{\partial h_n}{\partial a_n},\quad
\frac{\partial a_n}{\partial w},\quad
\frac{\partial a_n}{\partial b},
\]
then average over \(n=1,...,N\).


Answer

Let
\[
e_n=s_n-y_n.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial s_n}\left(\frac{1}{2}(y_n-s_n)^2\right)
=s_n-y_n=e_n,
\]
we have
\[
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial v}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N e_n h_n,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial c}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N e_n.
\]
Also,
\[
\frac{\partial s_n}{\partial h_n}=v,
\qquad
\frac{\partial h_n}{\partial a_n}=h_n(1-h_n),
\qquad
\frac{\partial a_n}{\partial w}=x_n,
\qquad
\frac{\partial a_n}{\partial b}=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial w}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N e_n v h_n(1-h_n)x_n,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{R}}{\partial b}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N e_n v h_n(1-h_n).
\]



32.0.3 Question 3
Recompute the forward pass for
\[
x=2,\quad y=1,\quad w=0.5,\quad b=0.1,\quad v=1.5,\quad c=-0.2,
\]
using \(a=wx+b\), \(h=\sigma(a)\), \(s=vh+c\), and \(L=\frac12(y-s)^2\).


Answer

The pre-activation is
\[
a=(0.5)(2)+0.1=1.1.
\]
Thus
\[
h=\sigma(1.1)=\frac1{1+e^{-1.1}}\approx 0.7503.
\]
The score is
\[
s=(1.5)(0.7503)-0.2\approx 0.9254.
\]
Finally,
\[
L=\frac12(1-0.9254)^2\approx 0.0028.
\]



32.0.4 Question 4
Carry the backward pass through the same scalar example from Question 3. Compute
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial s},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial v},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial c},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial h},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w},\quad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}.
\]


Answer

From the forward pass, \(h\approx0.7503\) and \(s\approx0.9254\). The loss derivative is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial s}=s-y\approx -0.0746.
\]
For \(s=vh+c\),
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial v}=(-0.0746)(0.7503)\approx -0.0560,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial c}= -0.0746,
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial h}=(-0.0746)(1.5)\approx -0.1119.
\]
For \(h=\sigma(a)\),
\[
\frac{\partial h}{\partial a}=h(1-h)\approx(0.7503)(0.2497)\approx0.1874,
\]
so
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a}\approx(-0.1119)(0.1874)\approx -0.0210.
\]
For \(a=wx+b\) with \(x=2\),
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}\approx(-0.0210)(2)=-0.0419,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\approx -0.0210.
\]



32.0.5 Question 5
After the backward pass in Question 4, gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta>0\) updates \(w\) by
\[
w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}-\eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial w}.
\]
Does this step increase or decrease \(w\) in the numerical example?


Answer

Here
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}\approx -0.0419<0.
\]
Therefore
\[
w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}-\eta(-0.0419)=w^{(t)}+0.0419\eta.
\]
For any \(\eta>0\), the update increases \(w\). This is consistent with moving opposite the gradient: a negative derivative means increasing \(w\) locally reduces the loss.



32.0.6 Question 6
Classify the update rule by its batch size. For a dataset of size \(N\), identify which case is full-batch gradient descent, which is strict stochastic gradient descent, and which is mini-batch gradient descent:
\[
|B_t|=N,\qquad |B_t|=1,\qquad 1<|B_t|<N.
\]


Answer

If \(|B_t|=N\), the update uses every training observation, so it is full-batch gradient descent.
If \(|B_t|=1\), the update uses one randomly selected observation, so it is stochastic gradient descent in the strict sense.
If \(1<|B_t|<N\), the update uses a subset larger than one but smaller than the whole dataset, so it is mini-batch gradient descent. As the lecture notes, neural-network practice often uses “SGD” broadly to include this mini-batch case.



32.0.7 Question 7
Hold \(\theta\) fixed. Assume a mini-batch of size \(B\) is sampled uniformly with replacement from the training indices \(\{1,\dots,N\}\). Let \(k_1,\dots,k_B\) denote the sampled indices, and define the mini-batch gradient as
\[
\hat g_B=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^B \nabla_\theta \ell(y_{k_j},s_\theta(x_{k_j})).
\]
Show that the expected value of this mini-batch gradient equals the full empirical-risk gradient:
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\nabla_\theta \hat R(\theta).
\]


Answer

For each training observation, define its individual gradient contribution as
\[
g_i=\nabla_\theta \ell(y_i,s_\theta(x_i)).
\]
Since \(k_1,\dots,k_B\) are sampled uniformly with replacement from \(\{1,\dots,N\}\), each sampled index \(k_j\) has the same distribution. Therefore, for each draw,
\[
\mathbb E[g_{k_j}]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i.
\]
The mini-batch gradient can be written as
\[
\hat g_B=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^B g_{k_j}.
\]
By linearity of expectation,
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^B \mathbb E[g_{k_j}].
\]
Substituting the expression for each \(\mathbb E[g_{k_j}]\) gives
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^B \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i\right).
\]
Since the same quantity is added \(B\) times,
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i.
\]
Now,
\[
\hat R(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \ell(y_i,s_\theta(x_i)).
\]
Taking the gradient gives
\[
\nabla_\theta \hat R(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_\theta \ell(y_i,s_\theta(x_i)).
\]
Using the definition of \(g_i\), this becomes
\[
\nabla_\theta \hat R(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N g_i.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathbb E[\hat g_B]=\nabla_\theta \hat R(\theta).
\]



32.0.8 Question 8
Suppose there are \(N=1250\) training observations and the mini-batch size is \(64\). How many updates are in one epoch if the algorithm uses every observation once and includes a final smaller mini-batch?


Answer

The exact number of updates is
\[
\left\lceil \frac{1250}{64}\right\rceil=20.
\]
There are \(19\) full mini-batches of size \(64\), which use \(19\cdot64=1216\) observations. This leaves \(1250-1216=34\) observations for one final smaller mini-batch.
So one epoch has \(20\) updates. The rough calculation \(1250/64\approx19.5\) suggests about \(20\) updates, and the exact count is \(20\) when the final partial mini-batch is included.



32.0.9 Question 9
In the chain
\[
x\to q\to r\to t\to u\to L,
\]
show explicitly how reusing \(\partial L/\partial r\) avoids recomputing the full chain-rule expression for \(\partial L/\partial q\).


Answer

The full chain-rule expression is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial u}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
\frac{\partial t}{\partial r}
\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}.
\]
But the first three factors are exactly
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial u}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}
\frac{\partial t}{\partial r}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}.
\]
Backpropagation stores or passes the already-computed derivative \(\partial L/\partial r\) and multiplies by only the next local derivative.



32.0.10 Question 10
At a single node \(r=f(q)\), suppose the incoming derivative is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}=5,
\]
and \(f(q)=q^3\) at \(q=2\). Compute the outgoing derivative \(\partial L/\partial q\).


Answer

The local derivative is
\[
\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}=f'(q)=3q^2.
\]
At \(q=2\),
\[
\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}=3(2)^2=12.
\]
The outgoing derivative is the incoming derivative times the local derivative:
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}
=5\cdot12=60.
\]



32.0.11 Question 11
Combine the local derivatives in the scalar graph to obtain a single formula for \(\partial J/\partial \alpha\) for one observation. Use
\[
J=\frac{1}{4}(u-t)^4,\qquad u=\gamma r+\delta,\qquad r=\tanh(q),\qquad q=\alpha z+\beta.
\]
Note: \(\tanh'(q)=1-\tanh^2(q).\)


Answer

The path from \(\alpha\) to \(J\) is
\[
\alpha \to q \to r \to u \to J.
\]
The chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial u}\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}\frac{\partial r}{\partial q}\frac{\partial q}{\partial \alpha}.
\]
The local derivatives are
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial u}=(u-t)^3,\qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial r}=\gamma,\qquad \frac{\partial r}{\partial q}=\tanh'(q),\qquad \frac{\partial q}{\partial \alpha}=z.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \alpha}=(u-t)^3\gamma\tanh'(q)z.
\]
Since \(\tanh'(q)=1-\tanh^2(q)\) and \(r=\tanh(q)\), this can also be written as
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \alpha}=(u-t)^3\gamma(1-r^2)z.
\]



32.0.12 Question 12
For a mini-batch \(B\) of scalar observations, let \(M=|B|\) and define
\[
J_B=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} L_n,
\]
where
\[
L_n=\frac{1}{4}(u_n-t_n)^4,\qquad u_n=\gamma r_n+\delta,\qquad r_n=\tanh(q_n),\qquad q_n=\alpha z_n+\beta.
\]
Write the gradients of \(J_B\) with respect to \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\).


Answer

Since
\[
J_B=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} L_n,
\]
each parameter gradient is the average of the corresponding single-observation gradients. First compute
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}=(u_n-t_n)^3.
\]
For compactness, define
\[
d_n=(u_n-t_n)^3.
\]
For \(\gamma\), the chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial \gamma}=\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial \gamma}=d_n r_n.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \gamma}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n r_n.
\]
For \(\delta\), the chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial \delta}=\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial \delta}=d_n.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \delta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n.
\]
For \(\alpha\), the path is \(\alpha\to q_n\to r_n\to u_n\to L_n\). The chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial r_n}\frac{\partial r_n}{\partial q_n}\frac{\partial q_n}{\partial \alpha}=d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n)z_n.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n)z_n.
\]
For \(\beta\), the path is \(\beta\to q_n\to r_n\to u_n\to L_n\). The chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial \beta}=\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial r_n}\frac{\partial r_n}{\partial q_n}\frac{\partial q_n}{\partial \beta}=d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \beta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n).
\]
Since \(\tanh'(q_n)=1-\tanh^2(q_n)\) and \(r_n=\tanh(q_n)\), the last two gradients can also be written as
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n\gamma(1-r_n^2)z_n,
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \beta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B} d_n\gamma(1-r_n^2).
\]



32.0.13 Question 13
For the mini-batch objective
\[
J_B=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}L_n,\qquad L_n=\frac{1}{4}(u_n-t_n)^4,
\]
with
\[
u_n=\gamma r_n+\delta,\qquad r_n=\tanh(q_n),\qquad q_n=\alpha z_n+\beta,
\]
why do the gradients for the shared parameters \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\) sum contributions over the mini-batch, while quantities such as \(\partial J_B/\partial r_n\) and \(\partial J_B/\partial q_n\) are kept separately for each observation before continuing backward?


Answer

The parameters \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\) are shared across all observations in the mini-batch. The same value of \(\gamma\), for example, appears in every expression
\[
u_n=\gamma r_n+\delta.
\]
Therefore, the total derivative of \(J_B\) with respect to \(\gamma\) must add the contributions from every observation:
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \gamma}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}\frac{\partial L_n}{\partial u_n}\frac{\partial u_n}{\partial \gamma}.
\]
Using \(d_n=(u_n-t_n)^3\) and \(\partial u_n/\partial \gamma=r_n\), this becomes
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \gamma}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}d_n r_n.
\]
The same idea applies to the other shared parameters. For example,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \delta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}d_n,
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \alpha}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n)z_n,\qquad
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial \beta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{n\in B}d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n).
\]
By contrast, \(r_n\) and \(q_n\) are not shared parameters. They are intermediate values for a specific observation \(n\). Before the backward pass can continue from \(r_n\) to \(q_n\), it needs one derivative for each observation:
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial r_n}=\frac{1}{M}d_n\gamma.
\]
Then, for each observation separately,
\[
\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial q_n}=\frac{\partial J_B}{\partial r_n}\frac{\partial r_n}{\partial q_n}=\frac{1}{M}d_n\gamma\tanh'(q_n).
\]
So the rule is: gradients for shared parameters are summed over the mini-batch, while gradients for per-observation intermediate quantities remain indexed by \(n\) until they are used by the next local backward rule.



32.0.14 Question 14
When a graph branches, gradient contributions add. Verify this in the concrete graph
\[
r=z^2,\qquad t=z^3,\qquad L=r+t.
\]
Compute \(\partial L/\partial z\) by adding path contributions, and compare with direct differentiation.


Answer

There are two downstream paths from \(z\) to \(L\). The contribution through \(r\) is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial r}\frac{\partial r}{\partial z}=1\cdot 2z=2z.
\]
The contribution through \(t\) is
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial t}\frac{\partial t}{\partial z}=1\cdot 3z^2=3z^2.
\]
Adding gives
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}=2z+3z^2.
\]
Directly, \(L=z^2+z^3\), so
\[
\frac{dL}{dz}=2z+3z^2.
\]
The two calculations agree.



32.0.15 Question 15
Consider the quadratic objective
\[
R(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\theta^2.
\]
For this objective, the gradient is
\[
R'(\theta)=\theta.
\]
Gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta\) therefore gives the update
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=\theta^{(t)}-\eta \theta^{(t)}.
\]
Assume \(\theta^{(0)}\ne0\).

What is the formula for \(\theta^{(t)}\) in terms of \(\theta^{(0)}\)?
For which values of \(\eta\) does \(\theta^{(t)}\) converge to \(0\)?



Answer

Starting from
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=\theta^{(t)}-\eta\theta^{(t)},
\]
factor out \(\theta^{(t)}\):
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}=(1-\eta)\theta^{(t)}.
\]
So in the form \(\theta^{(t+1)}=a\theta^{(t)}\), we have
\[
a=1-\eta.
\]
Applying the update repeatedly gives
\[
\theta^{(t)}=(1-\eta)^t\theta^{(0)}.
\]
This converges to \(0\) exactly when the multiplier \(1-\eta\) has absolute value less than \(1\):
\[
|1-\eta|<1.
\]
Solving this inequality gives
\[
-1<1-\eta<1.
\]
Subtracting \(1\) from all three parts gives
\[
-2<-\eta<0.
\]
Multiplying by \(-1\) reverses the inequalities:
\[
0<\eta<2.
\]
Therefore, gradient descent converges to \(0\) for learning rates satisfying
\[
0<\eta<2.
\]
If \(\eta>2\), then \(|1-\eta|>1\), so the iterates grow in magnitude. This is the precise sense in which a learning rate that is too large can make gradient descent unstable.



32.0.16 Question 16
Changing the mini-batch objective from an average
\[
\frac1{|B_t|}\sum_{n\in B_t}\ell_n(\theta)
\]
to a sum
\[
\sum_{n\in B_t}\ell_n(\theta)
\]
would change the gradient used in the update. What exactly changes, and why does the averaging convention make learning-rate comparisons across batch sizes cleaner?


Answer

The gradient of the sum is \(|B_t|\) times the gradient of the average:
\[
\nabla_\theta\sum_{n\in B_t}\ell_n(\theta)
=|B_t|\nabla_\theta\left(\frac1{|B_t|}\sum_{n\in B_t}\ell_n(\theta)\right).
\]
With the same learning rate, using the summed loss would therefore make the step size scale linearly with the batch size. Averaging keeps the gradient on roughly the same scale when \(|B_t|\) changes, so the learning rate has a more comparable meaning across different mini-batch sizes.
